title: How do you read a chart in a case interview and find the insight?
description: Exhibits are where cases are won or lost. A five-step routine for turning any chart into an insight.
hook: When an interviewer slides a chart across the table, it is tempting to start describing everything on it. That is the most common mistake. They want one thing: the insight that matters for the client. This guide gives you a short routine for reading any chart quickly and saying something useful about it.
body:
In this guide

  • Ask for a moment, then read in order
  • Insight, not description
  • Do the maths unprompted, and link back
  • A worked example
  • What to remember
  • Check yourself

Ask for a moment, then read in order

When you're handed a chart, say "May I take a moment?" and then read it in this order: title, axes and units, legend, and the footnote. Footnotes hide the answer surprisingly often: "excludes our new stores", "values in real terms".

Then follow five steps: read the chart, find what stands out, quantify it, link it to the goal, and say your next step.

Insight, not description

Weak candidates describe: "This shows supply and demand from 2026 to 2030." Strong candidates find what matters: "Demand overtakes supply from 2028, and by 2030 there's a 20% shortfall." Look for the biggest number, the biggest change, the crossing point, or the outlier.

Do the maths unprompted, and link back

If a number on the chart can be turned into something more useful (a percentage, a gap, a growth rate), do it without being asked. Then connect it to the goal in the box at the top of your page: "...which matters because our client legally needs 120,000 tonnes by 2030." Finish with where you'd go next.

See it in action: The five-step routine in one answer

"This shows bed occupancy for each of the client's 12 hospitals (1, read). Most sit between 60% and 78%, but three newer hospitals are around 40% (2, find the outlier). Those three drag the average down to 62% against a 75% benchmark (3, quantify). That matters because filling empty beds is the cheapest way to grow (4, link to goal). I'd like to understand why those three are empty: is it doctors or referrals? (5, next step)"

What to remember

  • Title, axes and units, legend, footnote, every time.
  • Lead with the insight, not a description.
  • Quantify it, link it to the goal, say where you’d go next.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer.

1. What should you read before drawing any conclusion from a chart?

  • Only the biggest bar
  • Title, axes, units, legend and footnote
  • Nothing: speed matters most
Show the answer

Title, axes, units, legend and footnote. Units and footnotes change the meaning of a chart more often than you’d think.

2. Which is an insight rather than a description?

  • "The chart shows sales by region."
  • "Sales fell in every region."
  • "Two-thirds of the drop comes from one region, the North."
Show the answer

"Two-thirds of the drop comes from one region, the North.". It locates the problem and tells you where to dig next.

Try it now

Sales by region, year 1 → year 2 ($M): North 40 → 28, South 35 → 36, West 25 → 26. Give one insight, with a number, and say where you’d look next.

Give yourself 60 seconds, out loud if you can.

Show a strong answer

"Total sales fell from 100 to 90, a 10% drop, but the North alone fell by 12, more than the entire decline, while the other regions grew slightly. So this is a North problem, not a company-wide one. Next I’d look at what changed in the North: a competitor, store closures or a key customer."
